related_questions.question: What stage of breast cancer is in the lymph nodes?

text_blocks.snippet: If breast cancer has spread to the lymph nodes, it is generally classified as Stage II or Stage III, depending on the extent of the spread and the size of the primary tumor. Specifically, Stage II means the cancer is either in the breast and/or nearby lymph nodes, while Stage III means the cancer has spread to more distant lymph nodes or surrounding tissues according to Cancer Research UK.

list.title: Stage II:
list.snippet: This stage is characterized by cancer that may be present in the breast and/or up to three lymph nodes under the arm (axillary lymph nodes). It can also be classified as Stage II if the tumor is a certain size (between 2cm and 5cm) and has spread to a few axillary lymph nodes.

list.title: Stage III:
list.snippet: This stage indicates that the cancer has spread to more lymph nodes (4 or more) or has spread to the lymph nodes near the breastbone (internal mammary lymph nodes). It can also be classified as Stage III if the tumor is larger than a certain size (e.g., 5cm) and has spread to a few axillary lymph nodes.

list.title: Stage IIIA:
list.snippet: This is the earliest form of Stage III breast cancer and involves the spread of cancer to 4-9 lymph nodes or the presence of cancer in the internal mammary lymph nodes.

list.title: Stage IIIB:
list.snippet: This stage includes tumors that have spread to the chest wall or skin of the breast.

list.title: Stage IIIC:
list.snippet: This stage involves cancer spread to 10 or more lymph nodes, including those under the collarbone.

text_blocks.snippet: It's important to note that the specific stage is determined by a combination of factors, including the size of the primary tumor, the number and location of affected lymph nodes, and whether the cancer has spread to other parts of the body (metastasis). A doctor will determine the exact stage based on these factors and other diagnostic tests.

text_blocks.snippet: Breast cancer is classified into stages 0 through 4, with stage 0 representing non-invasive cancer and stage 4 indicating metastatic cancer. Stages 1, 2, and 3 denote varying degrees of tumor size and spread to lymph nodes, with higher numbers indicating more extensive disease.
Here's a breakdown of the stages:

list.snippet: Stage 0 (Carcinoma in situ): Cancer cells are present but have not spread beyond their original location (ducts or lobules).
Stage I (Early Invasive): Cancer is small and may or may not have spread to nearby lymph nodes.
Stage II: Cancer is larger than in Stage I and may or may not have spread to lymph nodes. It can also be described as Stage IIA or IIB.
Stage III (Locally Advanced): Cancer has spread to lymph nodes and possibly surrounding tissues, but not to distant organs.
Stage IV (Metastatic): Cancer has spread to distant organs, such as the bones, liver, or lungs.

text_blocks.snippet: The staging system also incorporates the TNM system, which considers the tumor size (T), lymph node involvement (N), and metastasis (M).

list.snippet: T (Tumor): Ranges from TX (tumor cannot be assessed) to T4 (tumor has spread to chest wall or skin).
N (Nodes): Ranges from N0 (no lymph node involvement) to N3 (metastasis to many lymph nodes).
M (Metastasis): Ranges from M0 (no distant metastasis) to M1 (distant metastasis).
